body:
Discussed this with fellow Mozillians and we have some comments:

 - It may be tricky to correctly serialize the data coming out of a form especially as the form changes between sessions, for example generated names would make this trickier, as well as lack of field names or a form ID. So we agree, it would likely be a requirement that only forms with IDs can be persisted.
 - It might not be ideal to put this behind an API like `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`, instead we might opt to use a storage mechanism which is not web exposed due to various constraints: likely we don't want developers to modify the data, the storage may not always be guaranteed, etc. 
 - Browsers already have this concept, especially on mobile - where processes may shutdown and restore more aggressively. It might be worth trying to leverage or standardise the same mechanisms here, but this might limit the available scope of what we can expose.
 - There already exists the [`formStateRestoreCallback`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#custom-element-reactions:form-associated-custom-element-4) Custom Element Reaction, which is used when UAs attempt to restore or autofill a Form Associated Custom Element's field. Perhaps we can apply a similar level of abstraction for this case: perhaps a `restore` event on forms could be emitted by UAs at their own discretion, and web developers can use scripting to listen for the event and fill the relevant fields (which also allows developers to handle issues around migration/validation and so-on). This would allow developers to opt in via the event, rather than an attribute on the form.

Sorry I guess I didn't make it clear enough, but many things you mentioned was something I already stated.

Then let me clarify

> So we agree, it would likely be a requirement that only forms with IDs can be persisted.

- Yes, the `id` or `name` field is a requirement, I just wasn't sure which one would fit better, if you say `id` I'm fine. I also put `name` since that's how forms are indexed in `document.forms`>.

> It might not be ideal to put this behind an API like localStorage or sessionStorage, instead we might opt to use a storage mechanism which is not web exposed <...>

Yes, that's what I meant, I made the options `local` and `session` exceptionally for similarly to `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`. I also mentioned that form persistence should happen out of browser exposed API to be more secure and avoid aggressive storage cap.

I think this also goes with `namedItem` well since it uses either `id` or `name` (source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLCollection/namedItem).

> Browsers already have this concept, especially on mobile - where processes may shutdown and restore more aggressively. It might be worth trying to leverage or standardise the same mechanisms here, but this might limit the available scope of what we can expose.

- Yes, when you fill in form fields and accidentally close the window and then reopen, the data is restored. The problem is that it won't work for programmatically created inputs i.e. for every SPA app, which is very unfortunate.

> There already exists the `formStateRestoreCallback` Custom Element Reaction <...>

- I haven't seen that, will look into it.

---

> perhaps a `restore` event on forms could be emitted by UAs <...> This would allow developers to opt in via the event, rather than an attribute on the form.

Maybe. My intention of an attribute for form was so that you can have persistence without scripting, making it declarative. If this is not possible we can discuss other approaches to it, I'm open to everything, though my lovely variant would be a defined property, attribute, callable method for form restoration or API for form cache, accessible at will in browsers like

```js
const form = document.forms.myForm
form.persist = "local" // Not at `localStorage`, but between tabs for the same domain.
form.restore() // Data can be restored unless any input was made after form appeared or form submit/reset.
```

> [`formStateRestoreCallback`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#custom-element-reactions:form-associated-custom-element-4)

As per this link (at the moment I write this):

> When user agent updates a [form-associated custom element](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#form-associated-custom-element)'s value on behalf of a user or [as part of navigation](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#restore-persisted-state), its `formStateRestoreCallback` is called, given the new state and a string indicating a reason, "autocomplete" or "restore", as arguments.

This is related to the custom `HTMLFormElement` behavior and navigation, which is ok, however my proposal is to add a feature of persisting **named** inputs of **named** forms with least effort possible.

The persistence of forms already can be well done with scripts and `localStorage`. The proposal is to avoid scripting at all, so that pages that do not use JavaScript can also use form persistence.

You can imagine a website that handles form with PHP, so if form submitting, auto-filling, validating can be done without scripts, why it can't be persisted?

(In the future, please consider responding once, instead of four times, as each response sends an email to 700+ people. If this means waiting until you're at a computer, so you can give a more thoughtful response, that's even better. There is no need to respond to this message.)

Thanks @domenic, you gave me a fresh look at my proposal again.

Forms persistence may be User engaged instead of fully "automatic":

Named forms with named inputs (and with `persist`/`restorable` attribute) can be restored from User acceptance (not sure what UI should look like).
If a named form has `persist` attribute and User accidentally closes, for example, dynamically created popup with the form, which filling in took an hour. And then User opens the popup again with shaking hands, the browser would give a hint that User can restore his precious data. I imagine it as auto-filling when I choose my login from the list, which would also fill other fields (like email, password).

This behavior can be customized by listening to a form event (e.g. `restore`) and if `event.preventDefault` is called, user will be hinted nothing. This means custom hinting UI can be implemented by a developer and then if user clicks restore button in custom UI, `form.restore` can be called to confirm restoration.

Of course, another mechanism can be implemented, here's an alternative (I'm just brainstorming):
`restore` event would contain `FormRestorationRequest` e.g. in `event.restorationRequest`, which could be stored somewhere. It would be alive until form is submitted, reset or stale (let it be 1 week).

The interface may look like this
```ts
interface FormRestorationRequest extends AbortController {
  restore(): void // Restores form data.
  readonly lastEdited: number // Timestamp when the last edit to form inputs was made.
}
```

Edge case: User may introduce updates just after `restore` event fired, then `FormRestorationRequest` can be immediately aborted OR a little action window can be given until aborting the request, so that user could fill in some fields and restore other ones (though not sure if this useful).

This is based on this idea:

> There already exists the [`formStateRestoreCallback`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#custom-element-reactions:form-associated-custom-element-4) Custom Element Reaction, which is used when UAs attempt to restore or autofill a Form Associated Custom Element's field. Perhaps we can apply a similar level of abstraction for this case: perhaps a restore event on forms could be emitted by UAs at their own discretion, and web developers can use scripting to listen for the event and fill the relevant fields (which also allows developers to handle issues around migration/validation and so-on). This would allow developers to opt in via the event, rather than an attribute on the form.

---

Stepping from **`form`** events, `form` object can have an array of its unsubmitted versions.
If any present, a developer can implement custom UI for User-engaged OR script-based form data restoration. Not sure about **many** versions, one should go also (I'm just overthinking).

> [!NOTE]
> That this all happens only if `persist` or such attribute/property is present on `form` element.
> Form data restoration should happen only if developer meant this behavior beforehand.

@keithamus
I revised this proposal with more minimal and "closed" approach and leveraging already existing `formStateRestoreCallback`.

First, I would propose to make it subscriptable (`form.addEventListener("stateRestore")`) since it should be accessible for any form.

For context, the point is to let an HTML form to define how it should be restored (e.g. for a closable modal or SPA applications). Manual form persistence is costly, inconsistently implemented, and error-prone - this proposal aims to standardize the common case, especially for SPA applications as their rely on programmatic page updates.

## Minimal Proposal

Consider a form such as `<form name="bank-details">`, my intent as a developer to keep my users happy and fine-tune fields restoration in case of accidental actions that may wipe all their inputs. That's a lot of work and not so many companies/developers would invest so much time just to have this "simple" feature. I also realized that there should be minimum complexity to make sure developers are less prone to make mistakes restoring forms.

With this, I think if there was something like `<form name="bank-details" restorable>`, it would be just enough since all cases are the same: a form with a unique name that restores previous user inputs if it's gone and back.

So instead of unclearly setting `persist="local"`, we would rather mark a form as restorable, explicitly opting a form into UA-managed restoration.

Additionally, this default action could be overridden in `stateRestore` (projection of `formStateRestoreCallback`) event:
```js
form.addEventListener("stateRestore", event => {
  event.preventDefault()

  event.formName
  event.formState // Cloned FormData.
  event.target // Newly appeared form.
  event.currentTarget // => null. The event was fired by User-Agent not by form itself.

  // ... custom restoration.
})
```

However, some inputs may be irrelevant for restoration, a developer may decided that certain inputs should be omitted from restoration:

```html
<input name="csrf" type="hidden" restorable="false">
```

## Proposed high-level semantics

As you see, nothing fancy anymore, more straightforward, though it seems obvious that some details are still missing:
- what exactly `restorable` does for forms and inputs
- user inputs recording strategy
- user inputs persistence/storage
- user inputs invalidation
- user inputs mismatch
- when `stateRestore` is fired

Let me define those as I see it:
- a restorable form treats its inputs as `restorable` by default. If a form or an input sets `restorable="false"`, it's simply skipped from inputs **recording**.

- user inputs recording strategy may be to eagerly persist every named field (excluding `restorable="false"`) within a dictionary (a similar can be done in JS by listening to `change` on form and recording named elements and their values). It can be done per keystroke, word or be exactly how undo/redo works for `textarea` in Chrome.

- user inputs persistence/storage - the data should be stored in a storage similar to `localStorage` since there could be cases such as electricity outage or when any element, website, browser exits [^1]. Thus persistence should be sufficiently durable to survive common accidental data-loss scenarios (e.g., tab closure or crashes).

- user inputs invalidation - the data can't be stored forever, so it needs to be emptied eventually. I suggest to empty out when user successfully submitted [^2] or reset a form or together with scheduled browser site cache invalidation. Form inputs are not invalidated after restoration. If developer wants to invalidate programmatically, `stateRestore` event can be used to prevent fields population with `.preventDefault()`.

- user inputs mismatch - missing or extra fields should be ignored, restoring only those that were within a form when `restorable` attribute has been set or when an element was connected to the document [^3]. If a form was restored, but user had more interactions, all new inputs should be appended and existing ones overridden.

- `stateRestore` should be fired when a named restorable form with recorded inputs, which was previously disconnected, is connected again with the same name and `restorable` attribute. This attribute is vital, if a form with the same name appears without it, nothing should happen, but when a form gets `restorable` attribute - the restoration checkup should be invoked, which may fire the event.

I tried to cover as many things as I could and minimize this proposal as much as possible. I tried fitting this one in existing "walls" and now it seems feasible. As a starting point, this could be limited to a single feature: `<form name="..." restorable>` with UA-defined default restoration behavior and no events or input-level attributes. Additional hooks could be layered later if justified by experience.

Please, tell me if I need to provide more details, create a playground or maybe you'd like to discuss it f2f.

_I have a big interest in contributing to HTML/DOM/Web standards, perhaps you could give advice of what meetings I could attend related to whatwg in the next year. Thanks for reading, and Happy New Year!_

[^1]: It doesn't really matter if a browser tab was closed by a trusted user click because it may be accidental - a user misclicked, closed a modal, tab, browser or navigated to a different page.
[^2]: successfulness of submission is applicable for `action="..."`-based forms and if there are no errors in `submit` event - if action leads to a failed request/response or `submit` event has errors, user inputs are kept NOT invalidated.
[^3]: If a disconnected form gets `restorable` attribute, nothing happens, restoration checkup is only engaged when a named restorable form is attached to a document (probably excluding `DOMParser`).
